data.title: Trading Tens and Ones
data.description: Learn how to trade one ten block for ten ones to understand place value better.

challenges.instruction: Look at the blocks on your mat and predict what happens when you trade one ten for ten ones.
challenges.hint: Count your tens and ones. Remember that one ten is equal to ten ones.

challenges.instruction: Examine the blocks on the mat and predict the new total after making a trade.
challenges.hint: Check the tens place column. Trade one ten block to get ten more ones.

challenges.instruction: Predict the result before trading one of the tens for ten ones on your mat.
challenges.hint: Look closely at the tens column. One ten will break apart into ten ones.

challenges.instruction: Make your prediction for the new block arrangement after completing the trade.
challenges.hint: Count how many ones you will have after trading a ten.

plan.activityLine: read a block mat aloud and trade blocks between places

items.cue: [BT_ITEM] Scene: Block mat: 4 hundred-flats, 8 ten-sticks, 6 ones cubes. The trade under way is one hundred-flat for ten ten-sticks. Say exactly: "Let us trade some blocks. You tell me what will happen first, and then you make it happen. You have 8 ten-sticks. You are going to trade one hundred-flat for ten ten-sticks. How many ten-sticks will you have then?" Private expected count: 18. Judge only the current spoken prediction. Accept a number word or a short sentence such as "eighteen ten-sticks". The signature wrong answer is "ten" — the blocks the trade creates, with the ones already on the mat forgotten — and it is incorrect. The starting count on its own is also incorrect. Negated correct numbers and conflicting guesses are incorrect. If correct say exactly: "Yes, eighteen ten-sticks." If incorrect say exactly: "My turn: ten new ten-sticks arrive and eight were already there, so there are eighteen. Your turn. You have 8 ten-sticks. You are going to trade one hundred-flat for ten ten-sticks. How many ten-sticks will you have then?" A previous turn never answers the current question, even when the number would be the same. A verdict ends your turn: after the affirmation or the correction you stop, and you never continue into another question, another example, or an offer of more work.
